explainer.heading: What the poem says
explainer.body: Sarojini Naidu asks weavers what they weave at three times of day. At break of day they weave a bright blue robe for a new-born child; at fall of night, purple-and-green marriage veils of a queen; in the chill moonlight, a white funeral shroud for a dead man.
explainer.example: The three garments stand for birth, marriage (youth) and death — the three stages of life.
explainer.hook: Morning = birth, evening = marriage, night = death.

explainer.heading: Colours and moods
explainer.body: Blue (“as the wing of a halcyon wild”) — fresh, joyful start of life. Purple and green (“like the plumes of a peacock”) — royal, rich, colourful youth. White (“as a feather and white as a cloud”) — calm, peace, purity and the end of life. The mood moves from gay (cheerful) to solemn and still.

explainer.heading: Simile
explainer.body: A simile compares two unlike things using “like” or “as”: “Blue as the wing of a halcyon wild”; “Like the plumes of a peacock”; “White as a feather and white as a cloud”.

explainer.heading: Alliteration
explainer.body: Repetition of the same consonant sound in nearby words: “plumes of a peacock, purple”; “Weavers, weaving”; “solemn and still”; “garment so gay” (g).

explainer.heading: The poet
explainer.body: Sarojini Naidu (the “Nightingale of India”) was a 20th-century poet and freedom fighter, fluent in English, Urdu and other languages. Her first collection was “The Golden Threshold”.

questions.q: How does the poet show the three stages of human life through the work of the weavers?
questions.model: The weavers work at three times of day, matching three stages of life. At break of day (morning of life) they weave a bright blue robe for a new-born child — birth. At fall of night they weave purple and green marriage veils for a queen — youth and marriage, the rich, colourful middle of life. In the chill moonlight they weave a white shroud for a dead man — death. The mood changes from gay and bright to solemn and still.
